title: Super Mario World
japaneseTitle: スーパーマリオワールド
shortDescription: The Super Nintendo launch masterpiece that introduced dinosaur companion Yoshi, multi-exit secret level topology, and rich 16-bit acoustic sampling.
historicalSignificance: The defining launch title of the 16-bit era, selling over 20 million cartridges and introducing Yoshi, the Cape Feather flight mechanics, and the multi-path Star World secret hierarchy.

editorialContent.overview: Directed by Takashi Tezuka with production by Shigeru Miyamoto and an integrated musical score by Koji Kondo, Super Mario World debuted as the premier launch title for the Super Famicom in Japan on November 21, 1990 (August 1991 in North America). Designed to demonstrate the generational leap from the 8-bit NES to the 16-bit SNES, it transported Mario and Luigi to Dinosaur Land for an expansive, joyous platforming adventure.
editorialContent.gameplayMechanics: The signature gameplay breakthrough was the introduction of Yoshi, a friendly green dinosaur Mario can ride to swallow enemies, spit fireballs, and reach high secret ledges. Mario's mobility reached new heights with the Cape Feather, enabling acrobatic soaring and diving momentum. The 96 exit goals encouraged meticulous exploration, rewarding players who found alternate key-and-keyhole exits with secret warp routes across Star Road and the brutal Special World.
editorialContent.technicalInnovation: Super Mario World harnessed the SNES's Ricoh 5A22 16-bit processor and custom Picture Processing Units (PPU1/PPU2), displaying rich 256-color palettes, smooth multi-plane parallax background scrolling, transparency effects for ghost house lighting, and Sony SPC700 8-channel ADPCM sampled music.
editorialContent.culturalImpact: Bundled with millions of Super Nintendo consoles, Super Mario World sold over 20 million copies worldwide. Yoshi immediately became one of Nintendo's most beloved perennial superstars, starring in his own celebrated franchise.
editorialContent.preservationNotes: Preserved on authentic 512KB Super Nintendo cartridge dumps. Maintaining Sony SPC700 32kHz sample interpolation and proper 60.0988 Hz NTSC master clock timing is necessary for authentic audio and jump physics.
